summary.text: The disproof takes the formally included case \(n=0\): its divisor sums and totient give \(a(0)=0\), but \(0\) is neither \(1\) nor prime, contradicting the claimed characterization of equality.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\Bigl(\sigma_2(n)+\varphi(n)\sigma(n)-2n^2\Bigr)_{\ge 0},
\]
where \(\sigma_2(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d^2\), \(\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\), and \((x)_{\ge0}=\max(x,0)\) denotes conversion of the resulting integer to a natural number. In the formal statement being refuted, the quantifier ranges over every natural number, including \(0\). The definition used there adopts the conventions that the finite divisor set of \(0\) is empty and that \(\varphi(0)=0\).

We disprove that formal universal statement by taking
\[
n=0.
\]
Because the divisor set used in the definition is empty at zero, both divisor sums are empty sums. Hence
\[
\sigma_2(0)=\sum_{d\in\varnothing}d^2=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sigma(0)=\sum_{d\in\varnothing}d=0.
\]
Also \(\varphi(0)=0\), and of course \(2\cdot0^2=0\). Therefore the integer inside the final conversion is
\[
\sigma_2(0)+\varphi(0)\sigma(0)-2\cdot0^2
 =0+0\cdot0-0=0.
\]
Its nonnegative part is still zero, so
\[
a(0)=0.
\]

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the formalized conjecture were true for every \(n\in\mathbb N\). Its first asserted equivalence would then give, at \(n=0\),
\[
a(0)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (0=1\ \text{or}\ 0\text{ is prime}).
\]
The left-hand side is true by the computation above. Consequently the right-hand side would have to be true. There are two possible cases.

1. If \(0=1\), this is immediately false because zero and one are distinct natural numbers.

2. If \(0\) is prime, this is also false. Every prime natural number is greater than or equal to \(2\) (equivalently, is greater than \(1\)), whereas \(0\) is not greater than \(1\). Thus zero is not prime.

Both alternatives are impossible. Hence
\[
\neg\bigl(0=1\ \text{or}\ 0\text{ is prime}\bigr),
\]
even though \(a(0)=0\). The equivalence
\[
a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (n=1\ \text{or}\ n\text{ is prime})
\]
therefore fails at \(n=0\). Since the formal conjecture requires this equivalence, together with the separate characterization of the value \(2\), to hold for every natural number, failure of the first equivalence at this single value is enough to refute the entire conjunction. No analysis of the value-\(2\) assertion is needed.

This is a disproof of the formal statement quantified over all \(n\in\mathbb N\). It is important that it does not disprove the canonical OEIS conjecture as stated for \(n\ge1\): the sole counterexample used here is \(n=0\), which lies outside that stated domain. Thus the accepted argument exposes a missing positivity hypothesis in the formal formulation rather than a positive-integer counterexample to the original OEIS claim.
